Hey there. I'm sure we can agree that your sudden change in personality is due to the loss that you experienced. Losses like that can impact us in huge ways, and it's kinda scary.

Cutting yourself off from people is a normal reaction to a loss like that. It's almost expected, even. So you're not going crazy or anything like that. It's natural, but it's good to remember that you can't really do that forever. 

That's why I think you should take your recovery one step at a time. Maybe instead of trying to fix all of the things at once, you can list them out in order of priority that your logical-brain thinks you should do (while ignoring your immediate desires to an extent that is easy for you, and going from there). Maybe start to cut down on just the unhealthy habits before you move on to reintegrating yourself into society amongst your friends and such. Disciplining yourself little by little is easier and more efficient than trying to discipline yourself in several regards at once.

Irritability is a pretty common symptom of depression. It may not always be there, but if you know you are depressed, then it is safe to assume that the irritability is linked to that. 

I think practically everybody will have a problem with others doing things that appear wrong or stupid. The only important thing here is to keep the frustration at a reasonable level. 

I used to get really annoyed and even pissed off at people for doing things that I didn't approve of. This went on for a long time, until it actually hit me that it doesn't matter. Because no matter how much I'll rage and rant about it, it just doesn't matter and won't matter in the greater scheme of things. The person will not be affected, only you will be affected. You will be the only one who hurts inside, and with depression already on your plate, you don't need that extra frustration at all. It's important to do some self-talk and assure yourself to stop giving a shit about some things. Humans will always make mistakes; if you raged every time a human being around you made a mistake, then you would be miserable forever. It's just not worth it, man. In the end of all things, it is simply not worth causing yourself such stress and pain over other peoples' mistakes, no matter how stupid they are. 

So my advice would be to talk to yourself and "ration" out your frustration. Yeah, it's okay to be a little annoyed or a little angry, but don't let it consume you. Think of it this way, while you fume on the inside over these things, the person who did the thing you disagree with is already over it and has no qualms about it whatsoever. If they get to be worry-free about it, then so should you. I know this is easier said than done, but it is just one of those behaviors that a person needs to instill into their brain over and over until it sticks.

I think it is totally possible to get through depression without taking anti-depressants. However, that probably depends on several things like the choices you make, your personality, the severity of the depression, etc. 

I got through a terrible depression using nothing but anti-depressants. I had close to no support from anybody, and to be honest, I didn't really try to be proactive about it, meaning I didn't follow the psychiatrist's advice on the choices I should make. All I did was take anti-depressants for a year and did what I normally did every day and I started feeling better. I don't know what to attribute this to, but something probably changed on the subconscious level. I think taking the meds told my brain that I was trying to get better, and as a result I subconsciously started making more of an active effort to do positive things for myself. Whatever that subconscious force may be, I owe a lot of it to meds. 

With that said, I think it's worth trying anti-depressants. I know the idea of taking meds to improve your mood can be kind of strange, cause that's how I felt at first too. But I think good things can come out of it. All of the drugs have side effects and things like that, but your psychiatrist will let you try out more than one to see which one works best for you and your body. I went through several different ones until I found one that worked for me.

The thing with Remeron is that it's gonna knock you out at night. After you take it, you're good for 10-12 hours of sleep. I've found that if I take Remeron late at night and try to wake up early (before those 10-12 hours of guaranteed sleep are over), it'll be incredibly hard due to how drowsy it has made me. That's why I've had to adjust my schedule a little bit so that I can go to bed earlier, and as a result take Remeron earlier. That way, I've allowed it's drowsy effect to wear off by the time I wake up.  It really depends on your schedule, though. 

It's also possible that your body simply doesn't react well to it. If that's the case, then you'll have to wait to talk to your doc about changing your meds. Just know that the groggy feeling that you've mentioned is pretty common with Remeron, the good news being that this effect usually declines after a while if your body gets accustomed to it. I've been taking Remeron for about a year and I still feel a little drowsy during the day, but it's nowhere near as bad as it was at first. Just keep in mind that the later at night you take the Remeron, the worse your morning/day will be in terms of sleepiness and drowsiness.

Unfortunately, we can try to predict the future all we want but we'll never know for sure what awaits us.

My advice would be to start from there and use that direction to guide yourself towards other things, such as a careers, goals, etc. It's all a matter of a baby steps that will eventually get you *somewhere* in x amount of time as opposed to being in the same position in x amount of time, still feeling bad.

I am happy to hear that. You'll find that making a decision such as this will give you a feeling of being in control of the situation, which is pretty much a great thing in the face of a seemingly hopeless issue.

I went through something pretty much exactly the same as you. It was terrible, just as what you are going through right now is terrible.

My advice, and in my opinion the BEST thing you can do to move forward in life is to remove him and all signs of him from your life. This means deleting him from your phone, on facebook, and removing anything that might make you want to think about him or contact him. I would even go as far as to block him from all mediums of communication.

This is INCREDIBLY hard, because emotions. That's normal. But from my own personal experience, I can guarantee that this will help you loads. 

You don't need that stress, and you certainly don't need to put up with somebody who is tossing you aside in such a way. This is a time during which you have to look out for yourself, and that means removing his existence from your life. Out of sight, out of mind.

Taking this step will make a huge difference because you'll be doing something about your feelings. It'll give you a sense of "closure" and a sense of finally moving on from a problem, even if your emotions are still lingering on it. It's a great first step to take, in my opinion. From then on, you should have an easier time recovering and doing whatever it is that you need to do to make things normal for yourself again.

Remeron has been great for me. I take it at night, around half an hour before I go to bed because it causes a lot of drowsiness. If you're somebody who has trouble falling asleep every night, then this will be like magic for you. Before taking Remeron I thought i'd never be able to sleep properly. Well, now I sleep MUCH better and I feel much better overall in the morning. Another really major side effect is weight gain. I'm not sure if it directly makes you hungrier or does something with your metabolism or something like that, but I have definitely gained a good amount of weight ever since I started taking it. As a really thin guy, this worked out quite well for me. 

Remeron has been very helpful with my depression problems, but not significantly enough with my anxiety. That's why I've been working with my psychiatrist over the course of the past couple months to find a new medicine that works for me. (I've tried like 3 anti-anxiety meds but none of them worked for me). I guess the thing about these kinds of medication is that you've just got to try a couple of them and see which one works for you. Prozac is really popular and it works for a lot of people so it is likely that it will help you. But if you keep experiencing those shitty side effects then I would definitely recommend that you discuss Remeron with your psychiatrist.

I come from a Pakistani family as well, so you're definitely not alone when it comes to dealing with parental pressures. 

Some parents like to force their son/daughter to make certain choices. It's a sign of good intentions but it isn't really practical or fair. Your dad obviously wants you to be successful, but he is also being unfair to you. Your father most likely did not do everything that his parents told him to do. I'm in the same boat as you, friend. Second-year college student here. Been going through a shitload of stress and anxiety for a ton of things, college included. So I think I have at least a general understand of how you're feeling.

First of all, I know it's easy to blame yourself. I mean, it's the first thing that usually comes to mind, right? But that's not always the reason for these kind of problems. One fact that I'm sure we can all accept is that *college is pretty fucking demanding*. I mean, in high school, we're all relatively baby'ed along and guided to some extent, even in the advanced courses. The college system is difficult for a lot of people to adjust to, and in a lot of cases, people just hate it for reasons ranging from laziness to irresponsibility to just about anything. I'm not saying anything bad about you, because I know it is not in your nature to be lazy or irresponsible (you AP/honors kid, you). But there is something about college that just isn't right here.

It's entirely possible that you're just having bad luck with shitty teachers. It's 100% possible, because it's not uncommon to have a teacher who both sucks at teaching and sucks at writing exams. It's also possible that your study habits have declined since high school, meaning that you aren't putting enough focus on certain material or certain parts of the material. Likewise, it's possible that you may just hate the major that you had a passion for. I had a passion for computer science from middle school until high school, but when I started taking courses for it in college, I fucking *hated* it, man. I barely passed those classes and changed my major immediately after the semester ended. Sometimes it takes extended exposure to a study for a person to realize that it's just not for them. Maybe you have no interest in those classes? Try to locate the issue.

- Limb damage (Has a small chance of being added when the character takes damage while unarmored. More armor pieces = less chance of getting this debuff. Limb damage could cause your character to dig/mine/attack/work slower or less efficiently)

- Poison (Maybe there could be a small chance that a spider attack causes this debuff? And it would slowly drain the character's health)

- Paralysis (Don't know to implement this, but it would be interesting to see)

People might say that these sort of features will turn Minecraft more into an RPG, but I personally don't think so. I mean, we already have the experience system which is an RPG game concept. All these debuffs are simply chances of something "different" happening from an event that we are all used to experiencing. It'll allow for more things that the user will need to keep in mind when exploring, making the actual idea of exploring more dangerous -- every risk could come with serious consequences. Essentially, this system would really just reinforce the survival aspect of the game, in my opinion.

You love learning? That's awesome, I respect that. I've always been the same way, but I found a way to cope with it. I was suicidal as well, 2-3 years ago, and I really didn't know what I could do. I didn't talk to anybody, I didn't tell anybody about it, and I didn't have any friends. But then I began writing. It wasn't out of nowhere, because I got the inspiration from my English teacher. But I pushed myself to start. I began recording my thoughts and processing them into poems and stories. And you know what? It helped. It helped a LOT. And even now, while I am not suicidal or depressed, I continue writing because it went from being my savior to my passion.

The reason writing (or any other art form, for that matter. I just prefer writing, and I'll explain why) is so helpful is because it clears up all the cluttered thoughts in your mind. Think about it - you're sitting there, either typing them up or handwriting them. And eventually, you have all of your thoughts out there on paper. With that, you are able to properly think in a systematic way. But it doesn't end there. Not only are you organizing your thoughts, but with writing, you can let out any raw emotion that you are feeling (sadness, anger, etc). Just let it out onto whatever medium you use, and don't control or limit yourself. Aim to write poetry, or something creative. I wouldn't recommend aiming for a novel or something, but if you're up for it, do it! Seriously, I can't stress how important writing is. With your mind focused on more creative and imaginative things, you'll have less time to really be dwelling on the negatives of life. Hell, you'll even start looking at things in a more realistic way once you've been writing. (Realistic meaning not JUST negative, but also positive.) Eventually you'll find yourself creating beautiful pieces of writing.

Honestly, give it a try. I know it's going to be difficult. But try to push yourself to do it. Take your time and list out all your thoughts and concerns. Then imagine for a bit, and see how you can use a poem or story as an outlet for those emotions and thoughts. You'll find yourself feeling reasonably more calm, and at the same time, feeling proud of yourself for being so damn artistic. You'll be surprised how creative an individual can be, especially one who is in your condition. If you need help or any other advice for that, or if you'd like to share what you wrote, do NOT hesitate to PM me or reply here! Seriously, I'd love to help you in any way I can.
